message.content:
**United States – Gini Coefficient (most recent estimates)**  

| Year | Source | Gini (pre‑tax) | Gini (after‑tax) |
|------|--------|----------------|------------------|
| 2022 | World Bank (World Development Indicators) | **0.421** | — |
| 2021 | OECD (Income Distribution Database) | **0.410** | — |
| 2020 | U.S. Census Bureau (Current Population Survey) | **0.485** (pre‑tax) | **0.395** (after‑tax) |

> **Interpretation**  
> The Gini coefficient ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality). A value of ~0.42 indicates that the United States has a moderate level of income inequality, higher than many European countries but lower than many developing economies.

### Why the numbers differ

| Factor | Effect on Gini |
|--------|----------------|
| **Pre‑tax vs. after‑tax** | Taxation and transfers reduce inequality, so after‑tax Gini is lower. |
| **Data source & methodology** | The U.S. Census uses household survey data; the World Bank uses national accounts; OECD aggregates national accounts and survey data. |
| **Year of data** | Income distribution can shift year‑to‑year; the most recent World Bank figure (2022) is the latest global estimate. |

### Quick Takeaway

- **Current (2022) pre‑tax Gini**: **≈ 0.42**  
- **After‑tax Gini** (latest U.S. Census estimate, 2020): **≈ 0.39**  

These figures place the U.S. in the middle range of global income inequality. If you need the Gini for a specific year or a different methodology (e.g., wealth Gini), let me know!
